null-vs-empty-query.name: Null vs Empty Query Object
null-vs-empty-query.description: One parser returns null (no query) while another returns an empty object/dict {} when the URL has no query string or only a fragment delimiter.

percent-encoding-in-keys.name: Percent-Encoding Differences in Keys
percent-encoding-in-keys.description: Parsers differ in whether they decode percent-encoded characters (especially control characters like %09, %0A, %0D) in query key names.

duplicate-key-array-vs-string.name: Duplicate Key: Array vs String
duplicate-key-array-vs-string.description: When the same key appears multiple times in the query string, one parser stores values as an array while another keeps only one value as a string.

no-value-key-null-vs-empty-string.name: No-Value Key: null vs Empty String
no-value-key-null-vs-empty-string.description: For keys without a value (e.g. ?key or ?key=), one parser stores the value as null while another stores it as an empty string "".

plus-decoded-as-space.name: Plus Sign Decoded as Space in Keys
plus-decoded-as-space.description: Some parsers decode '+' as a space character in query key names (application/x-www-form-urlencoded behavior), while others leave '+' as a literal plus sign.

dot-in-key-replaced.name: Dot in Key Name Replaced
dot-in-key-replaced.description: Some parsers (notably PHP's parse_str) replace dots and spaces in key names with underscores, while others preserve the original dot characters.

whitespace-in-key-normalized.name: Whitespace/Control Characters in Keys Normalized
whitespace-in-key-normalized.description: Some parsers (notably PHP's parse_str) replace whitespace and control characters (tabs, newlines, carriage returns) in key names with underscores, while others preserve the literal characters.

no-value-key-dropped.name: No-Value Key Dropped vs Kept
no-value-key-dropped.description: When a query parameter has no `=` sign (e.g. `?foo&bar=1`), some parsers (e.g. PHP's parse_str) retain `foo` as a key with an empty string value, while others (e.g. Python's urllib3) silently drop the key entirely.

bracket-notation-key-mangled.name: Bracket Notation in Key Name Mangled
bracket-notation-key-mangled.description: Some parsers (notably PHP's parse_str) interpret `[` in query key names as PHP-style array bracket notation, stripping or transforming the bracket portion, while others treat `[` as a literal character and preserve it in the key name.

key-ordering.name: Key Ordering Difference
key-ordering.description: Parsers return the same query keys and values but in a different order, reflecting differences in internal data structure ordering (insertion order vs. sorted, etc.).

empty-key-included-or-dropped.name: Empty Key Included or Dropped
empty-key-included-or-dropped.description: When a query string contains a delimiter that produces an empty key name (e.g. `?&foo=1`, `?foo&&bar=1`, or `?=val`), some parsers include the empty string `""` as a key while others silently drop it.

semicolon-separator.name: Semicolon as Query Parameter Separator
semicolon-separator.description: Some parsers (e.g. Perl's URI, older CGI libraries) treat semicolons (`;`) as alternative parameter separators equivalent to `&`, splitting the query string on `;` in addition to `&`, while others treat `;` as a literal character within a key or value.

crlf-stripped-from-keys.name: CRLF/Tab Stripped from Query Keys
crlf-stripped-from-keys.description: Some parsers (following the WHATWG URL standard) strip CR (`\r`), LF (`\n`), and TAB (`\t`) characters from query strings before parsing, causing those characters to disappear from key names, while others preserve them as-is.
